title: Microsoft Expands Circular Centers to Give Retired Azure Servers New Life
excerpt: Eight Circular Centers across three continents now securely decommission retired Azure hardware, hitting a 92% reuse and recycling rate as the AI buildout accelerates.
body:
• Microsoft now operates eight Circular Centers across North America, Europe and Asia Pacific — dedicated facilities that securely decommission retired Azure servers and decide each component's next useful life. New sites in Newport, Wales and Sydney, Australia were added this year, with a San Antonio, Texas center planned.
  • Microsoft achieved a 92% reuse and recycling rate for decommissioned servers and components last year, up from 90.9% in 2024, when it beat its own 2025 target of 90% a year early. More than 3.2 million components were reused in 2024 alone.
  • The network runs on the Intelligent Disposition and Routing System (IDARS), an AI-driven platform paired with Dynamics 365 that sorts end-of-life hardware, optimizes logistics routing and issues disposal instructions to operators while enforcing data-security compliance.
  • For enterprises, the program feeds Microsoft's zero-waste-by-2030 commitment and gives Azure customers verifiable hardware-reuse metrics for ESG reporting — a concrete data point for procurement teams evaluating cloud providers on sustainability.

Microsoft is expanding its network of Circular Centers — specialized facilities that take apart decommissioned Azure servers and give their components a second life —. With new facilities in Newport, Wales and Sydney, Australia, the network now spans eight centers across North America, Europe and Asia Pacific, and a ninth is planned for San Antonio, Texas.

The company said it achieved a 92% reuse and recycling rate for retired servers and components last year, building on the 90.9% rate reported for 2024, which beat Microsoft's own 2025 target of 90% a full year early.

What Circular Centers are

Every generation of cloud hardware eventually retires. As new AI-capable systems go in, older servers come out — millions of them across Microsoft's more than 60 cloud regions. Circular Centers manage that transition: the first opened in Amsterdam in 2020, Dublin and Boydton, Virginia followed in 2022, and the network has since grown to the US, Ireland, Singapore, Wales and Australia.

https://x.com/adlenesifi/status/2105631317379395770

Retiring a server is more involved than sorting parts into recycling bins. Every machine is formally decommissioned and its data-bearing components wiped before anything else happens. Triage sends complete systems to Microsoft labs and training environments, schools and universities, or qualified buyers for continued use; individual components become spare parts for other systems; materials are recycled only when reuse is no longer possible.

AI-driven triage behind the scenes

Underpinning the operation is the Intelligent Disposition and Routing System, or IDARS — an end-to-end planning platform paired with Microsoft Dynamics 365 that uses AI and machine learning to sort end-of-life assets, optimize logistics routes and hand operators precise disposal instructions, all while maintaining compliance and data security. Microsoft is adding AI-powered robotic disassembly and autonomous material handling to accelerate recovery.

A separate pilot tackles rare earth minerals: working with Western Digital and recycling partners, Microsoft has processed roughly 50,000 pounds of end-of-life hard drives, recovering neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, gold and copper — with about 95% fewer emissions than traditional mining. The program is partly funded through Microsoft's internal carbon tax, which charges business units a fee based on their emissions.

"By redesigning systems to reduce waste, then reusing and recovering materials wherever possible, we're saving costs, gaining efficiency and discovering new opportunities for hardware and infrastructure components."

— Rani Borkar, Corporate Vice President, Azure Hardware Systems and Infrastructure, Microsoft

Why it matters in the AI buildout

Microsoft frames circularity as efficiency: since 2014, cores per rack across Azure infrastructure have increased roughly 13-fold while the power required to complete the same task has fallen by about 90%.

For enterprise buyers, the program is also an ESG asset. Microsoft has committed to becoming carbon negative, water positive and zero waste by 2030,.

"Through material recovery — extracting valuable components from discarded products and putting them to work in new ways, like memory chips and motherboards — we're not just reducing waste, we're conserving resources and lowering emissions."

— Melanie Nakagawa, Chief Sustainability Officer, Microsoft

Diaspora angle

The program touches India's tech workforce twice over. Indian engineers make up a large share of the cloud-infrastructure and data-center workforce globally, including teams managing Azure hardware lifecycles. And with Microsoft now running four Azure regions in India, Indian enterprises on Azure inherit the same sustainability credentials for their own ESG reporting.

What's next

The San Antonio center will extend the network further across the United States, and robotic disassembly will scale up recovery rates. The company's 2026 Environmental Sustainability Report is expected to update the reuse figures. As AI capacity keeps climbing, the question for every hyperscaler is whether end-of-life hardware becomes a cost center or a resource — Microsoft is betting heavily on the latter.
